title: Cups to Grams Converter (Flour, Sugar, Oil) | Hacé Cuentas
h1: Convert Cups to Grams for Baking
description: Instant cups to grams converter: flour (120g), sugar (200g), oil (220g). Free, accurate, covers 18 baking ingredients based on King Arthur Baking + USDA data.
intro: This converter translates cup measurements into grams for the most common baking ingredients — all-purpose flour, bread flour, whole-wheat flour, granulated sugar, powdered sugar, packed brown sugar, vegetable oil, olive oil, butter, honey, milk, and more. Because a cup is a volume unit (240 mL in US recipes) while grams measure mass, the conversion factor depends entirely on the ingredient's density. For example, 1 cup of all-purpose flour weighs approximately 120 g, while 1 cup of honey weighs 340 g — a 183% difference for the exact same volume. Density factors are drawn from the King Arthur Baking Ingredient Weight Chart and USDA FoodData Central, the two most-cited sources in professional recipe development. Use this tool whenever a recipe lists cups but your kitchen scale (or a professional recipe) requires grams for precise, reproducible results.
keyTakeaway: **Grams = Cups × Density Factor (g/cup)** — e.g., 2.25 cups all-purpose flour = 2.25 × 120 g = **270 g**; 1 cup granulated sugar = **200 g**; 1 cup vegetable oil = **220 g**. Always spoon flour into the cup and level with a straight edge — never scoop from the bag.
useCases: Scaling a bread recipe that lists 3 cups of whole-wheat flour to grams for a digital kitchen scale: 3 × 130 g = 390 g.
Converting a US cake recipe to metric units for baking in Europe or Australia, where cup volumes differ from the 240 mL US standard.
Precisely measuring cake flour for a sponge cake where ±10 g affects crumb texture and rise.
Doubling or halving a cookie recipe and needing exact gram equivalents to avoid compounding measurement errors.

example.title: Example: 2¼ cups all-purpose flour for chocolate chip cookies
steps: Classic chocolate chip cookie recipes call for 2¼ cups of all-purpose flour.
Result: 270 g. If you had scooped the cup directly into the bag (~150 g/cup), you would have used 337 g — 67 g too much, producing a dry and crumbly cookie.

explanation:
## How It's Calculated

The formula is straightforward:

```
Grams = Cups × Density Factor (g per cup)
```

Each ingredient has a fixed density factor derived from King Arthur Baking's weight chart and USDA food composition data. The factor accounts for how tightly particles pack inside a standard 240 mL US cup at room temperature.

## Reference Table (1 US cup = 240 mL)

| Ingredient | g/cup | ½ cup | ¼ cup | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| All-purpose flour (spooned & leveled) | 120 | 60 | 30 | King Arthur |
| Whole-wheat flour | 130 | 65 | 32.5 | King Arthur |
| Almond flour | 96 | 48 | 24 | King Arthur |
| Granulated white sugar | 200 | 100 | 50 | King Arthur |
| Brown sugar (packed) | 220 | 110 | 55 | King Arthur |
| Powdered / icing sugar | 120 | 60 | 30 | King Arthur |
| Unsweetened cocoa powder | 85 | 42.5 | 21.25 | King Arthur |
| Vegetable oil | 220 | 110 | 55 | USDA |
| Extra-virgin olive oil | 216 | 108 | 54 | USDA |
| Butter (solid) | 227 | 113.5 | 56.75 | USDA |
| Whole milk | 240 | 120 | 60 | USDA |
| Honey | 340 | 170 | 85 | USDA |
| Rolled oats (quick-cook) | 90 | 45 | 22.5 | King Arthur |
| Rolled oats (old-fashioned) | 80 | 40 | 20 | King Arthur |
| Chocolate chips | 170 | 85 | 42.5 | King Arthur |
| Shredded coconut (dry) | 80 | 40 | 20 | King Arthur |
| Uncooked rice | 195 | 97.5 | 48.75 | USDA |

> **Note:** Flour values assume the spoon-and-level method. Scooping directly from the bag packs the cup and can add 20–30 g per cup (up to +25%).

## Common Mistakes

1. **Scooping flour directly from the bag.** This packs the cup and adds 20–30 g per cup, resulting in dense, dry baked goods. Always spoon flour into the cup and level with a straight edge.
2. **Assuming all sugars weigh the same.** Granulated sugar (200 g/cup), powdered sugar (120 g/cup), and packed brown sugar (220 g/cup) differ by up to 83%.
3. **Treating a 250 mL cup as a US cup.** Australian/Canadian/metric cup = 250 mL adds ~4% extra per cup. Accumulated across multiple ingredients in a recipe, that error compounds.
4. **Not packing brown sugar.** Loosely filled brown sugar weighs only ~160 g/cup vs. 220 g when firmly packed — a 37% difference that noticeably dries out cookies and cakes.

faq.q: How many grams is 1 cup of all-purpose flour?
faq.a: 1 cup of all-purpose flour weighs approximately 120 grams using the spoon-and-level method, according to the King Arthur Baking Ingredient Weight Chart — the standard reference used by most professional recipe developers in the US. If you scoop the flour directly from the bag, the cup can pack to 150 g or more — a 25% overshot that leads to dense, dry baked goods.

faq.q: Why do cups and grams give different results for different ingredients?
faq.a: A cup measures volume (240 mL in the US), while grams measure mass. Each ingredient has a unique density — how much mass fits into that fixed volume. Honey (340 g/cup) is nearly three times as heavy as rolled oats (80 g/cup) for the same cup volume, because honey is a dense liquid while oats are airy flakes. This is why volume measurements are inherently less precise than weight measurements in baking.

faq.q: Is 1 cup the same in all countries?
faq.a: No. A US legal cup = 240 mL, an Australian/Canadian metric cup = 250 mL, and an old imperial UK cup = 284 mL. That's a 4–18% volume difference. If you follow a US recipe using a 250 mL metric cup, each cup of flour will be 12.5 g heavier than intended. Always check a recipe's country of origin and use the corresponding cup size — or just convert everything to grams.

faq.q: Does it matter if brown sugar is packed or not?
faq.a: Yes — significantly. A loosely filled cup of brown sugar weighs roughly 160–170 g, while a firmly packed cup reaches 220 g — a 30% difference. Most US recipes specify 'packed' brown sugar. When converting to grams, use 220 g per packed cup. Press the sugar down firmly with your fingers and level the top.

faq.q: Do sifted and unsifted flour weigh the same per cup?
faq.a: No. Sifting aerates flour, reducing density. Unsifted all-purpose flour (spoon-leveled) weighs ~120 g/cup; sifted all-purpose flour weighs ~108–110 g/cup — about 10% less. The recipe's phrasing matters: '1 cup sifted flour' means sift then measure, while '1 cup flour, sifted' means measure then sift. These yield different amounts.

faq.q: How do I convert grams back to cups?
faq.a: Simply reverse the formula: Cups = Grams ÷ Density Factor. For example, 300 g of all-purpose flour ÷ 120 g/cup = 2.5 cups. 400 g of granulated sugar ÷ 200 g/cup = 2 cups. This is especially useful when your scale gives you the total weight and you need to communicate the amount in cups.

faq.q: Why are oil cup-to-gram conversions important for calorie tracking?
faq.a: Oils are calorie-dense: olive oil provides approximately 884 kcal per 100 g (USDA). At 216 g per cup, a single cup of olive oil contains roughly 1,910 kcal. Even a 2-tablespoon (1/8 cup) error equals ~27 g of oil and ~239 extra kcal. For anyone tracking macros or calories, converting oils from cups to grams before calculating is far more accurate than relying on volume alone.

faq.q: What is the best technique for measuring flour by cup if I don't have a scale?
faq.a: Use the spoon-and-level method: (1) fluff the flour in its container with a spoon, (2) spoon flour into the measuring cup until overflowing, (3) level the top with a straight-edge knife. Never shake, tap, or scoop the cup into the bag. This technique consistently produces cups closest to the 120 g/cup standard used by King Arthur Baking and most US recipe developers.

faq.q: How many tablespoons are in a cup, and how do I use that for partial conversions?
faq.a: 1 cup = 16 tablespoons = 48 teaspoons. So 1 tablespoon = 1/16 of a cup. To convert tablespoons to grams: multiply the tablespoon count by the ingredient's g/cup factor, then divide by 16. Example: 3 tablespoons of butter = (3/16) × 227 g ≈ 42.6 g. This is useful for small quantities where entering a decimal cup (0.1875 cups for 3 tbsp) feels unwieldy.
